 Daylight Saving Time 
 The time change is near. What to know as daylight saving time ends Sunday 
 By the time daylight saving time ends, Chicago will still be losing about two minutes and 30 seconds of daylight each day, with sunset occurring at 4:44 p.m. on Nov. 1, according to TimeandDate. 
 By Matt Stefanski and NBC Chicago Staff • 
 Published 6 hours ago • 
 Updated 6 hours ago 
 BOOKMARKER 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Iisha Scott has a breakdown of what the sunset times in the Chicago area look like before daylight saving time ends and after. 
 The days are getting shorter and sunsets are coming earlier, with another sign of the changing seasons just around the corner.
 Illinois will “fall back” one hour on Sunday, when daylight saving time ends.

 Daylight saving time is the period when clocks are moved forward in the spring. When it ends, clocks return to standard time.
 Under the Energy Policy Act of 2005, daylight saving time begins on the second Sunday in March and ends on the first Sunday in November, with clocks moving forward in the spring and back in the fall.
 This year, daylight saving time ends Nov. 1, when clocks turn back one hour at 2 a.m.
 Earlier sunsets are on the way, but so is an extra hour of sleep.
 By the time daylight saving time ends, Chicago will still be losing about two minutes and 30 seconds of daylight each day, with sunset occurring at 4:44 p.m. on Nov. 1, according to TimeandDate.

 As November progresses, the amount of daylight lost each day will gradually decrease. By the end of the month, Chicago will see just nine hours and 23 minutes of daylight.
 The earliest sunsets of the year will arrive in early December. By the winter solstice on Dec. 21, Chicago will have just over nine hours of daylight, before the days gradually begin getting longer.
 Daylight saving time is scheduled to resume March 14, 2027, but that's not certain. 
 The House passed legislation this summer that would make daylight saving time permanent, though the Senate has yet to take up the measure.
 If the legislation ultimately becomes law, the twice-yearly changing of the clocks could become a thing of the past.
